cards.q: What is the DOM, in one sentence, and what is React's relationship to it?
cards.a: The DOM is the tree of objects the browser builds from your HTML, which JavaScript can read and mutate. React is not an alternative to it — every React update ends as ordinary DOM operations. React only decides which operations to run.

cards.q: Before frameworks, why did the amount of update code grow faster than the app?
cards.a: Because you hand-write a path for every pair of (thing that can change, part of the screen that depends on it). Ten pieces of data and fifteen pieces of screen is a web of transitions, each of which you must remember to write.

cards.q: What does it mean to say 'application truth leaked into the DOM', and why is it dangerous?
cards.a: Facts like "is the modal open" or "is the empty-state showing" end up discoverable only by inspecting DOM classes or styles. The DOM becomes an undesigned second database with no schema that any code, extension, or CSS transition can mutate behind your back.

cards.q: What is the characteristic bug shape of hand-written DOM syncing?
cards.a: Two parts of the screen disagree, because one update path fired and its sibling did not. The counter says 3 of 7 while the list shows 4 completed.

cards.q: Did jQuery solve this problem?
cards.a: No. It made each individual DOM operation shorter and cross-browser safe, but it did not reduce the number of transitions you had to write. The failure was never verbosity — it was that the developer owned every transition between every two screen states.

cards.q: State the gap Node 0 leaves in one sentence.
cards.a: You are forced to write transitions ("when this changes, go edit that") when what you actually know is destinations ("given this data, the screen should look like this").

cards.q: Why does the number of components in an app not predict its complexity in the pre-React model?
cards.a: Complexity comes from the number of data-to-screen dependencies, not the number of screen pieces. Adding one filter multiplies the conditions inside every existing update path.

cards.q: Why is 'the DOM is slow' an incomplete explanation of why React exists?
cards.a: Because React does not avoid DOM work — it performs the same operations. The problem React solves is authoring: who is responsible for deciding which operations run. Speed is a secondary, sometimes negative, effect.

cards.q: What is the one-sentence contract every framework in this space offers?
cards.a: Describe the screen as a function of data, and we will keep the DOM in agreement with it.

cards.q: When and by whom was React open-sourced?
cards.a: 29 May 2013, by Jordan Walke at Facebook, announced at JSConf US. It was already running in production in Facebook Ads and Instagram.

cards.q: What is a React element? Be precise.
cards.a: An ordinary, immutable plain JavaScript object that describes what should be on screen — roughly { type: 'li', props: { className: 'task', children: 'Buy milk' } }. It is not a DOM node, it is not on the page, and creating one is nearly free.

cards.q: What is the difference between a React element and a DOM node?
cards.a: An element is a plan; a DOM node is the building. Elements are cheap immutable descriptions React throws away and rebuilds every update; DOM nodes are expensive live objects React keeps and mutates minimally.

cards.q: What does React.createElement(type, props, ...children) return?
cards.a: A React element object. It does not touch the DOM and does not render anything — it only builds the description.

cards.q: What is JSX, mechanically?
cards.a: A syntax extension compiled before the browser sees it into createElement (or _jsx) function calls. It is not HTML and not a template language — it is sugar over function calls.

cards.q: Why is it className and not class in JSX?
cards.a: Because JSX compiles to a JavaScript object of props, and class is a reserved word in JavaScript. The same reasoning gives camelCase onClick, tabIndex, htmlFor.

cards.q: What do curly braces mean inside JSX?
cards.a: "Stop parsing markup, evaluate this JavaScript expression, use its value." Not string interpolation.

cards.q: Why can't you write {if (x) ... } inside JSX?
cards.a: if is a statement, not an expression, and braces accept only expressions. Hence the idioms cond ? a : b and cond && a.

cards.q: Why must a component return a single root element?
cards.a: Because a JSX tree compiles to a single function call, and a function returns one value. Fragments exist to satisfy this without extra DOM.

cards.q: What is a fragment and when do you need the long form?
cards.a: <>...</> groups children without producing a DOM node. You need the long form <React.Fragment key={id}> when the fragment is a list item and needs a key — the short syntax accepts no props.

cards.q: What changed about JSX compilation in React 17?
cards.a: The new JSX transform (October 2020) compiles JSX to _jsx() auto-imported from react/jsx-runtime, so files no longer need import React from 'react' just to use JSX. A missing React import is a quick tell that a file is post-17.

cards.q: Why are react and react-dom separate packages?
cards.a: react owns elements, components, and hooks — renderer-agnostic. react-dom knows about the browser. The same core drives React Native and other renderers, so the description layer must not depend on the DOM.

cards.q: What is the modern entry point for a React app, and what did it replace?
cards.a: createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />), introduced in React 18 (March 2022). It replaced ReactDOM.render(...). Which one a codebase uses tells you instantly whether it has been migrated.

cards.q: What is the 'virtual DOM' and why is the name misleading?
cards.a: The in-memory tree of element descriptions React diffs against the previous one. The name invites the belief that it is a speed technique — it is not. It is a correctness technique: the screen is re-derived from data every time, so it cannot drift.

cards.q: Is the virtual DOM faster than hand-written DOM manipulation?
cards.a: No. A single well-chosen el.textContent = 'x' by a careful human beats building and diffing objects. You trade peak performance for a guarantee that the screen cannot disagree with the data.

cards.q: What values render as nothing in JSX?
cards.a: null, undefined, false, and true. Strings and numbers render as text — which is why 0 shows up on screen.

cards.q: State React's core inversion in one sentence.
cards.a: You produce a description of the screen; React produces the DOM operations that make reality match it.

cards.q: Why does React re-create the entire element description on every update rather than patching it?
cards.a: Because elements are cheap immutable objects. Rebuilding is simpler to reason about than incrementally maintaining a description, and the expensive part — the DOM — is still only touched where the descriptions differ.

cards.q: What does dangerouslySetInnerHTML do and why the name?
cards.a: Sets raw HTML on a node, bypassing React's escaping. The name is deliberately alarming because it reopens cross-site scripting: any user-supplied string in it can inject script.

cards.q: How does React protect against XSS by default?
cards.a: Values interpolated into JSX are escaped as text, so {'<script>'} renders as visible characters, not markup. The escape hatch is dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

cards.q: What is StrictMode in one line, and does it ship to users?
cards.a: A development-only wrapper that double-invokes renders and effects to surface impurity and missing cleanups. It has no effect in a production build.

cards.q: How do you write an inline style in JSX and why the double braces?
cards.a: style={{ color: 'red' }} — the outer braces are JSX's 'expression follows' and the inner ones are an object literal. Keys are camelCase because they are JavaScript properties.

cards.q: What is a component, by definition?
cards.a: A function that takes one object argument (props) and returns a React element. Nothing more — there is no class, registration, or base type required.

cards.q: Why must component names be capitalised?
cards.a: <TaskRow /> compiles to createElement(TaskRow, ...) passing the function; <taskRow /> compiles to createElement('taskRow', ...) passing a string. React branches on string-vs-function to decide DOM tag or your component, and the compiler branches on the first letter's case.

cards.q: What are props and how do they arrive?
cards.a: A single object holding everything the parent passed. Destructuring in the parameter list — function Row({ title, done }) — is the universal style.

cards.q: Is children special?
cards.a: No. It is an ordinary prop that React fills with whatever you nested between the opening and closing tags. That is what makes wrapper components like <Card> possible.

cards.q: What can be passed as a prop?
cards.a: Anything a JavaScript object property can hold: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, objects, functions, and React elements themselves.

cards.q: Why must props be treated as read-only?
cards.a: React's entire update strategy assumes rendering is pure — same inputs, same output, nothing mutated. React does not deeply freeze props in production, so mutation appears to work and then produces haunted behaviour later.

cards.q: State the purity rule for rendering.
cards.a: Given the same props and state, a component returns the same elements and changes nothing outside itself: no mutating arguments, no writing to outer variables, no DOM edits, no network calls during render.

cards.q: Why does React insist data flows one way?
cards.a: Because when a value on screen is wrong, it came from exactly one place — the component directly above — so you can walk up the chain to find the lie. In the pre-React model, any of forty places could have written it.

cards.q: How does a child communicate upward if data only flows down?
cards.a: The parent passes a function down as a prop; the child calls it. Data down, events up. The child announces that something happened and never knows what it means.

cards.q: Why does 'data down, events up' make components reusable?
cards.a: Because the child holds no knowledge of consequences. TaskRow does not know whether delete removes from an array, sends a request, or opens a confirmation — so it drops into any of those contexts unchanged.

cards.q: What is the difference between a component and an element?
cards.a: A component is the function; an element is the object produced by calling it in JSX. TaskRow is a component, <TaskRow /> evaluates to an element describing it.

cards.q: Why does {items.length && <List/>} print a stray 0?
cards.a: When the array is empty, 0 && ... evaluates to 0, and React renders the number 0 as text — unlike false/null, which render nothing. Write items.length > 0 && ....

cards.q: What are the two idiomatic conditional rendering forms and why only these?
cards.a: cond ? <A/> : <B/> and cond && <A/>, because JSX braces accept only expressions, and both are expressions.

cards.q: How do you render a list in JSX?
cards.a: Map the array to elements: {tasks.map(t => <Row key={t.id} task={t} />)}. Arrays of elements are valid children.

cards.q: What is the gap Node 2 leaves?
cards.a: The app is a photograph. Nothing inside it can cause an update — components have no memory, since local variables die when the function returns.

cards.q: What is the difference between composition and inheritance in React, and which does React recommend?
cards.a: Composition — passing components and elements as props/children. React explicitly recommends it over inheritance; there is no idiomatic case for extending one component from another.

cards.q: What are default prop values in a function component?
cards.a: Default parameters in the destructure: function Btn({ size = 'md' }). The old Component.defaultProps is removed for function components in React 19.

cards.q: What is prop drilling?
cards.a: Passing a value through many intermediate components that do not use it, purely to reach a deep descendant. It works, but makes refactoring painful — which is the motivation for context.

cards.q: How do you type props in TypeScript, minimally?
cards.a: An interface or type for the props object: function Row({ id, title }: { id: string; title: string }), or a named type RowProps. No React.FC needed and it is generally discouraged.

cards.q: Why is spreading props (<Btn {...rest} />) both useful and risky?
cards.a: Useful for pass-through wrappers around DOM elements. Risky because it makes the component's real contract invisible and can forward unexpected attributes to the DOM, producing React warnings about unknown props.

cards.q: What does const [count, setCount] = useState(0) actually do?
cards.a: Asks React — the thing calling your function — to hold a value keyed to this component instance and hand it back on every later call. The value lives in React's internal record, not in your function.

cards.q: Why can't you just use a normal let for state?
cards.a: A local variable is recreated on every call of the function, so it resets on every render. And assigning to it would not tell React that anything changed.

cards.q: Why does calling setCount(count + 1) twice only increment by one?
cards.a: count is a const holding a snapshot of state at the start of this render. Both calls compute the same number. Use the updater form setCount(c => c + 1) when the new value depends on the old.

cards.q: Why does console.log(count) right after setCount print the old value?
cards.a: Because count is a constant in the current render's scope and setters do not assign to it. The new value appears in the next render, where useState returns it.

cards.q: When should you use the updater form of a setter?
cards.a: Whenever the next value depends on the previous one, or when the update may be queued alongside others. React applies queued updater functions in order against the latest value.

cards.q: What does calling a state setter actually do?
cards.a: Schedules a re-render. It is a request, not an assignment, and it does not synchronously re-run your component.

cards.q: How does React decide whether a state update is worth re-rendering?
cards.a: It compares the new value to the current one with Object.is. If they match it may bail out entirely — which is exactly why mutating an object and setting the same reference back renders nothing.

cards.q: Why does todos.push(x); setTodos(todos) not update the screen?
cards.a: You handed back the same array reference, so Object.is says nothing changed. Create a new value: setTodos([...todos, x]).

cards.q: How do you update one field of an object in state?
cards.a: Spread into a new object: setUser({ ...user, name }). Never assign into the existing object.

cards.q: What library exists to make immutable updates look mutable, and why?
cards.a: immer. Deeply nested spread updates get unreadable fast; immer lets you write mutating-looking code against a draft and produces a new object underneath. Redux Toolkit uses it internally.

cards.q: What is batching?
cards.a: Multiple setter calls in one handler produce exactly one re-render, not one each. React collects them and processes them together before painting.

cards.q: What changed about batching in React 18?
cards.a: Automatic batching everywhere. In React 17 and earlier, batching only happened inside React's own event handlers — updates in setTimeout, promise callbacks, or native listeners each caused their own render.

cards.q: Name and define the three phases of a React update.
cards.a: Render — React calls your components to build the new description; pure, may run more than once or be discarded. Commit — React applies the computed DOM operations. Paint — the browser draws pixels, in a later frame.

cards.q: What is the browser's frame budget and why does the number matter?
cards.a: About 16.7 milliseconds, which is one frame at 60 frames per second. Everything React does in a single blocking pass eats into it, which is what concurrent rendering later fights for.

cards.q: If you render <Counter /> twice, do they share state?
cards.a: No. State is keyed to the component's instance — its position in the tree — not to the function. Two positions, two independent states.

cards.q: Can you call a state setter during render?
cards.a: Not in general — it makes render impure and usually loops. The one sanctioned exception is the rare 'adjust state during render' pattern where you set state on the same component before returning, and React re-renders immediately without painting.

cards.q: What is the lazy initialiser form of useState and why does it exist?
cards.a: useState(() => expensiveInit()). The plain form useState(expensiveInit()) evaluates the argument on every render even though the value is only used on the first — passing a function defers it to the first render only.

cards.q: Is state synchronous or asynchronous?
cards.a: Neither word is quite right. The setter returns immediately without changing the current render's value; React processes queued updates and re-renders afterwards. Say "the setter queues an update and the new value is visible in the next render."

cards.q: Predict: a component calls setState with the same primitive value it already has. What happens?
cards.a: React compares with Object.is, sees no change, and may skip re-rendering entirely. It may still render once more before bailing out, but the DOM is untouched.

cards.q: You call three setters in a promise callback in React 17 versus React 18. Difference?
cards.a: React 17: three separate renders, because batching only covered React's own event handlers. React 18: one render, because batching is automatic everywhere.

cards.q: Why does an infinite render loop usually happen?
cards.a: Setting state during render, or an effect with no dependency array (or an unstable dependency) that sets state — each render triggers the effect, which triggers a render.

cards.q: Is it safe to store a function in useState?
cards.a: Only via the updater form, since useState(fn) treats fn as a lazy initialiser and setState(fn) treats it as an updater. Use useState(() => fn) and setState(() => fn).

cards.q: Why doesn't React use a general tree-diffing algorithm?
cards.a: Optimal tree diffing is too slow to run sixty times a second. React trades optimality for two heuristics that hold almost always in UIs, and gets a fast, predictable algorithm.

cards.q: State React's two reconciliation assumptions.
cards.a: 1) Elements of different types produce different trees. 2) The developer can supply stable identity for list children via key.

cards.q: What happens when the element type at a position changes?
cards.a: React destroys the entire old subtree — DOM nodes and all component state inside it — and builds the new one from scratch. No reuse is attempted.

cards.q: What happens when the element type at a position stays the same?
cards.a: React keeps the existing DOM node, updates only the attributes that actually differ, and recurses into children.

cards.q: State is tied to what, exactly?
cards.a: The component's position in the tree, not its name and not its props. Same type at the same position means the same instance and the same state.

cards.q: Why does wrapping a form in a conditional wrapper wipe what the user typed?
cards.a: {editing ? <Panel><Form/></Panel> : <div><Form/></div>} changes the type at that position, so React destroys the subtree and the Form's state with it. Keep the shape identical and state survives.

cards.q: You switch <Message user={a}/> to <Message user={b}/> and the half-typed reply carries over. Why, and what is the fix?
cards.a: Same type, same position, so React reuses the instance and its state. Fix: key={user.id}, which deliberately forces a fresh instance.

cards.q: How does React match children without keys?
cards.a: By index — first old child to first new child, and so on. Insert at the front of a thousand rows and every index shifts, so React treats every row as changed.

cards.q: What are the rules for a good key?
cards.a: Stable across renders for the same item, unique among siblings (not globally), and derived from the data — normally a database id.

cards.q: When is key={index} actually correct?
cards.a: Only when the list is never reordered, never filtered, and items are only ever appended at the end. Otherwise it is worse than no key.

cards.q: Why is key={index} worse than no key at all when items are deleted?
cards.a: It actively lies. After deleting the first item, the item now at index 0 claims to be the same thing that was there before, so React keeps the old DOM node and its state and only swaps the text — leaving checkboxes, focus, and input values attached to the wrong row.

cards.q: Why is key={Math.random()} wrong?
cards.a: A new key every render means every row is a different item, so React destroys and recreates the whole list each time — losing focus and DOM state and running slower than having no key.

cards.q: Can a component read its own key?
cards.a: No. React consumes it and it is not passed as a prop. If the child needs the id, pass it twice: <Row key={t.id} id={t.id} />.

cards.q: What is fiber and what did it replace?
cards.a: The internal linked structure of work units introduced in React 16 (26 September 2017), replacing React 15's plain recursive reconciliation. Because React walks it itself rather than using the JavaScript call stack, rendering can be paused and resumed.

cards.q: Did fiber change how you write React?
cards.a: No — it was invisible at the API level. It made concurrent rendering (transitions, deferred values, Suspense for data) possible, which arrived years later in React 18.

cards.q: Give the two-line rule for diagnosing 'my component state reset unexpectedly'.
cards.a: Ask whether the element type at that position changed, or whether its key changed. One of the two is nearly always the answer.

cards.q: Does changing a key on a component remount it?
cards.a: Yes — a different key means a different item, so React unmounts the old instance (running effect cleanups) and mounts a fresh one with initial state. This is the sanctioned way to reset a component.

cards.q: You reorder a list and the wrong row shows a spinner. Diagnose.
cards.a: Index keys. The spinner is DOM/component state attached to a position rather than to an item, so it stayed behind while the data moved. Switch to stable ids.

cards.q: Do keys need to be globally unique?
cards.a: No — only unique among siblings in the same array. Two different lists may both use key 1.

cards.q: What happens to effects when React destroys a subtree during reconciliation?
cards.a: All cleanup functions in that subtree run, in the same pass, before the new subtree mounts and its effects run.

cards.q: Why does React warn about missing keys instead of just using index silently?
cards.a: Because index matching is only safe under conditions React cannot verify. The warning asks you to assert identity, since only you know whether the list reorders.

cards.q: What is wrong with onClick={handleClick()}?
cards.a: It calls the function during render and passes the return value as the handler. The effect is a handler that fires once on render and never again.

cards.q: How do you pass an argument to an event handler?
cards.a: Wrap it: onClick={() => remove(task.id)}. The arrow function is the handler; it calls yours with the argument.

cards.q: What is a SyntheticEvent and why does it exist?
cards.a: React's own object wrapping the browser's native event. It originally existed to normalise genuine cross-browser differences in 2013, and remains because React needs one consistent event system across renderers. The native event is at e.nativeEvent.

cards.q: What was event pooling and what happened to it?
cards.a: Before React 17, React reused one synthetic event object and nulled its fields after the handler returned, so reading e.target in an async callback gave null and people called e.persist(). React 17 removed pooling entirely — that advice is obsolete.

cards.q: Does React attach a listener to every element with an onClick?
cards.a: No. It attaches a small number of listeners at the root and uses event delegation, relying on native bubbling, then simulates capture and bubble phases along the component path itself.

cards.q: Where were React's delegated listeners attached before and after React 17?
cards.a: Before 17: on document. From 17: on the root container element — so two React versions, or React embedded in a non-React page, can coexist without stealing each other's events.

cards.q: Why might e.stopPropagation() in React not stop a listener you added on document?
cards.a: Because they are two stacked systems. React's synthetic propagation is simulated inside React's own root listener; a native listener higher up still receives the real bubbled event.

cards.q: What is a controlled component?
cards.a: An input whose value comes from React state and whose changes write back to state: <input value={q} onChange={e => setQ(e.target.value)} />. The DOM never owns the truth.

cards.q: Why is a controlled input worth one render per keystroke?
cards.a: Because the value becomes ordinary data available to the whole app for free — character counts, disabled submit buttons, live validation, debounced search, a clear button — instead of being locked inside a DOM node.

cards.q: What is an uncontrolled component and when is it the right choice?
cards.a: The DOM keeps the value; you supply defaultValue and read it on submit, usually via a ref. Right for large forms you only read once — less code, far fewer renders. React Hook Form is built on this.

cards.q: What happens if you pass value without onChange?
cards.a: The field is frozen — React resets it to the state value on every render — and React logs a warning telling you to supply onChange or use defaultValue/readOnly.

cards.q: What causes the 'changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled' warning?
cards.a: value was undefined on the first render and a string later, usually from state initialised to undefined or data arriving async. Initialise to ''.

cards.q: How does React's onChange differ from the DOM's change event?
cards.a: React's fires on every keystroke (it is closer to the native input event). The native change event fires on blur. React deliberately renamed the semantics.

cards.q: How do you stop a form from navigating the page away?
cards.a: <form onSubmit={e => { e.preventDefault(); ... }}>. React does not change default browser behaviour here.

cards.q: Why should the submit handler live on the form and not the button?
cards.a: So keyboard submission (Enter in a text field) and implicit submission also work, and so validation runs once regardless of how the user submitted.

cards.q: How do you handle many inputs with one handler?
cards.a: Give each a name and use it as a key: setForm(f => ({ ...f, [e.target.name]: e.target.value })).

cards.q: How do checkboxes differ from text inputs in React?
cards.a: They use checked instead of value, and you read e.target.checked. Same controlled/uncontrolled distinction otherwise.

cards.q: What is the gap Node 5 leaves?
cards.a: State declared inside one component is invisible to its siblings. A header filter and a body list both need the query, and duplicating it makes them disagree — the Node 0 bug rebuilt at a higher level.

cards.q: How do you read a file input's value in React?
cards.a: With a ref or e.target.files — file inputs cannot be controlled, because their value is read-only for security reasons.

cards.q: Why does typing feel slow in a large controlled form, and what are the two fixes?
cards.a: Every keystroke re-renders the whole form. Fix by isolating the input into its own small component that owns its state, or by going uncontrolled — which is exactly React Hook Form's design.

cards.q: How do you handle a <select multiple> in React?
cards.a: Pass an array to value, and read the selected options from the event target to build the new array. React special-cases select so you never set selected on options.

cards.q: Why is onChange not firing for a controlled input you set from outside React?
cards.a: Because programmatically setting input.value on the DOM node does not dispatch React's synthetic event. React only knows about changes it originated or real user input.

cards.q: What does 'lifting state up' mean?
cards.a: Moving state to the nearest common ancestor of everything that needs it, then passing the value down as a prop and the setter down as a prop. Neither child owns it, so they cannot disagree.

cards.q: What is the single most useful test for whether something should be state?
cards.a: Can I compute it from other state or props? If yes, compute it during render. visibleTasks, total, isEmpty, fullName, hasErrors are all derived, not state.

cards.q: Why is storing derived values in state a bug and not just waste?
cards.a: Because you must then write an update path to keep it in sync with every input — the Node 0 disease. Recomputing is cheap and always correct; a cached copy is fast and eventually wrong.

cards.q: What is duplicated state? Give the classic example.
cards.a: Storing the same fact twice. Keeping selectedTask (the whole object) alongside tasks — edit the task in the array and the selection shows stale data. Store selectedId and look it up.

cards.q: What is contradictory state and how do you eliminate it?
cards.a: Booleans that can be true together but shouldn't be — isLoading, isSuccess, isError. Replace with one variable: status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'. This is the seed of the reducer node.

cards.q: Props versus state, in one line each.
cards.a: Props are what a component is told. State is what a component remembers.

cards.q: Why is useState(props.value) usually a bug?
cards.a: It captures the prop on the first render only and ignores every later change, producing "the parent updated but the child didn't." If you genuinely need a reset, change the child's key.

cards.q: How do you deliberately reset a child's state when a prop changes?
cards.a: Give the child a key derived from that prop. Changing the key remounts it with initial state — declarative, and no effect required.

cards.q: What structural pattern falls out of good state placement?
cards.a: State gets pushed up; components get pushed down. Stateless components that are pure functions of props are trivially testable and reusable.

cards.q: What were 'container' and 'presentational' components?
cards.a: An older naming for the split between components that hold state and fetch data and components that only render props. The terminology has faded; the instinct behind it has not.

cards.q: Where should state live — the general rule?
cards.a: As low in the tree as possible, but no lower than the closest common ancestor of everyone who reads it. Lower means fewer components re-render.

cards.q: What is the gap Node 6 leaves?
cards.a: The app is a closed world. It can only compute screens from data it already has — no fetching, no storage, no timers, no subscriptions, no measurement — because rendering was defined as pure.

cards.q: You have tasks, filter, and visibleTasks in state. What is the fix and why?
cards.a: Delete visibleTasks and compute it during render from the other two. Storing it requires an update path for every change to either input, which will eventually be missed.

cards.q: When is it acceptable to keep derived data in state?
cards.a: Essentially never for correctness reasons. If the derivation is genuinely expensive, keep it derived but wrap it in useMemo — that caches without creating a second source of truth.

cards.q: How do you decide the common ancestor for lifted state?
cards.a: Find every component that reads or writes the value, then take the lowest node in the tree that is an ancestor of all of them. Going higher than that costs unnecessary re-renders.

cards.q: When does useEffect's function run?
cards.a: After React has committed the DOM and the browser has painted. Your render stayed pure, the screen is already correct, and only then do you touch the outside world.

cards.q: What are the three parts of a useEffect call?
cards.a: The effect function; an optional returned cleanup function; and the dependency array that decides when it re-runs.

cards.q: What do the three dependency-array forms mean?
cards.a: No array — after every render. [] — after the first render only. [a, b] — after the first render and whenever a or b changed, compared with Object.is.

cards.q: Why does an effect with an object or function in its deps re-run every render?
cards.a: Because those are recreated fresh on every render, so Object.is says they changed. The fix is to stabilise them (useMemo/useCallback) or to depend on primitive fields instead.

cards.q: State the correct mental model for effects.
cards.a: Synchronisation, not lifecycle. An effect declares an ongoing relationship: "while roomId is X, this component should be connected to room X." Cleanup is the second half of that sentence, not an afterthought.

cards.q: Why is 'useEffect with [] means componentDidMount' a harmful framing?
cards.a: It makes you think about when the effect runs instead of what it depends on. That merges unrelated concerns into one effect and produces wrong dependency arrays — most notably forgetting the case where a dependency changes while the component stays mounted.

cards.q: What does StrictMode do to effects in development?
cards.a: Mounts the component, runs effects, immediately runs the cleanups, then runs the effects again. Development only — it never happens in a production build.

cards.q: You see two network requests in development. Is React broken?
cards.a: No. StrictMode's double-invoke is showing you an effect that is not a correct synchronisation — it fires once with no cleanup. The same bug would appear later on a real remount. Fix the effect; do not add a ref guard.

cards.q: Name four cases where you should not write an effect.
cards.a: Transforming data for display (do it during render). Responding to a user action (put it in the handler). Resetting state when a prop changes (use key). Computing something expensive from props (use useMemo).

cards.q: Why is 'effect watches state A and sets state B' a bad pattern?
cards.a: It causes a second render every time, is always wrong on the first render, and can cascade. Compute B during render instead.

cards.q: What are effects legitimately for?
cards.a: External systems: network, timers, browser APIs, subscriptions, the DOM outside React's tree, third-party widgets, analytics. Nothing else.

cards.q: What is useLayoutEffect and when do you need it?
cards.a: It runs after DOM mutation but before the browser paints. Use it when you must measure and adjust in the same frame to avoid a visible flicker — a tooltip deciding whether it fits above the button. Avoid otherwise: it blocks painting.

cards.q: What is useSyncExternalStore for?
cards.a: Subscribing to a store outside React (added in React 18). It exists because with concurrent rendering a naive subscription can let two parts of one screen read two different versions of the same store — a failure called tearing.

cards.q: What is useEffectEvent and what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Added in React 19.2 (October 2025). It lets an effect read the latest value of something without re-running when it changes. Before it, the workaround was storing the value in a ref, which you will see all over existing code.

cards.q: How do you cancel a subscription or timer correctly?
cards.a: Return a cleanup from the effect that undoes exactly what the effect did: clearInterval, removeEventListener, socket.close(), controller.abort(). React runs it before the next run and on unmount.

cards.q: What does the exhaustive-deps lint rule enforce and should you suppress it?
cards.a: That every reactive value used inside the effect appears in the deps. Suppressing it is almost always hiding a stale-closure bug — restructure the effect instead.

cards.q: What is a stale closure in the context of effects?
cards.a: An effect (or handler) captured a value from an old render and keeps using it after state has moved on — classic with setInterval and an empty dep array reading a counter that never updates.

cards.q: Predict: an effect with [] reads count inside a setInterval. What goes wrong?
cards.a: The interval callback closes over count from the first render forever, so it always sees the initial value. Fix with the updater form, or by listing the dependency and recreating the interval.

cards.q: Why does the order of multiple effects in a component matter?
cards.a: They run in declaration order after commit, and their cleanups run in the same order before the next run. If one effect depends on another's side effect having happened, that ordering is the only guarantee you have — and relying on it is a smell.

cards.q: When do effects run relative to a parent's and child's commit?
cards.a: Child effects run before parent effects — React commits the whole tree, then runs effects bottom-up, so a parent can rely on its children having synchronised.

cards.q: How do you run an effect only on updates and not the first render?
cards.a: Guard it with a ref initialised to true and flipped after the first run. It is a legitimate but rare pattern, and usually a sign the logic belongs in an event handler instead.

cards.q: List the four things wrong with a naive fetch-in-useEffect.
cards.a: Race conditions on rapid dependency changes; no error handling; contradictory loading/error/data state; and network waterfalls. Plus no caching, deduplication, or revalidation.

cards.q: Explain the race condition precisely.
cards.a: Change id from 1 to 2 quickly and two requests are in flight. If request 1 resolves after request 2 — normal, since network ordering is not guaranteed — you render user 1's data on a page labelled user 2.

cards.q: How do you fix the fetch race condition?
cards.a: Cleanup. Either set an ignore flag captured in the effect and check it before setting state, or call controller.abort() on an AbortController in the returned cleanup, so responses belonging to a stale render are discarded.

cards.q: What does the fetch race condition prove about cleanup functions?
cards.a: That cleanup is not bookkeeping or leak-prevention — omitting it is a correctness bug that renders the wrong data.

cards.q: What is a network waterfall and why is it invisible in code review?
cards.a: A parent fetches, then renders a child that fetches, so the child's request cannot start until the parent's returns. Three levels means three sequential round trips instead of one parallel batch. You only see it on a network timeline.

cards.q: Why do separate loading, error, and data states cause bugs?
cards.a: There is always a render where two of them disagree — the Node 6 contradictory-state problem. Every serious data library models one status value instead.

cards.q: What is the framing that justifies TanStack Query or SWR?
cards.a: Server data is not your state — it is a cache of someone else's state, so it needs different rules: keys, deduplication, background revalidation, staleness, retries.

cards.q: Name five things a data library gives you that hand-rolled fetching does not.
cards.a: Deduplication of identical in-flight requests; caching by key; background revalidation; retries with backoff; and shared results across components with one request.

cards.q: What is the use() API?
cards.a: A React 19 API that accepts a promise (or a context) and suspends the component until it resolves, integrating data loading with Suspense boundaries instead of with boolean flags. Unlike hooks, it may be called conditionally.

cards.q: What are Actions in React 19?
cards.a: A packaging of the pending/error/optimistic pattern for submissions and mutations, exposed through useActionState, useFormStatus, and useOptimistic, with form action props accepting async functions.

cards.q: What does useOptimistic do?
cards.a: Shows the expected result of a mutation immediately, then reconciles with the real result — or reverts automatically if it fails.

cards.q: How do you avoid a waterfall when a parent and child both need data?
cards.a: Hoist the requests so they start together — fetch both at the parent, or use a router/framework that declares data requirements per route ahead of rendering. Server components remove many waterfalls by doing the work in one place on the server.

cards.q: How do you cancel an in-flight fetch properly?
cards.a: Create an AbortController in the effect, pass controller.signal to fetch, and call controller.abort() in the cleanup. Catch and ignore the resulting AbortError.

cards.q: What is stale-while-revalidate?
cards.a: Show the cached value immediately, fetch fresh data in the background, then update. It is the default strategy of SWR and TanStack Query and is why navigating back feels instant.

cards.q: What is a query key and why does it matter?
cards.a: The identity of a cached request — usually an array like ['user', id]. It controls deduplication, cache hits, and invalidation; getting it wrong is the usual cause of 'the data didn't refresh'.

cards.q: Where should a mutation's cache invalidation happen?
cards.a: In the mutation's success handler, invalidating the query keys whose data the mutation could have changed — so the affected screens refetch rather than every component guessing.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: What does useRef(initial) return, and what are its two defining properties?
cards.a: A plain mutable object { current: initial } that React preserves across renders. Mutating ref.current does not trigger a re-render, and reading it during render is not safe because React does not track it.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: State the difference between state and a ref in one line.
cards.a: State is remembered and rendered; a ref is remembered and ignored.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: What are the two distinct uses of refs?
cards.a: Holding a value between renders that the screen does not depend on (an interval id, a previous value, a 'has run' flag), and holding a real DOM node.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: How do you get a DOM node, and when is it set?
cards.a: <input ref={inputRef} />. React sets inputRef.current to the element after commit and back to null on unmount — so read it in effects and handlers, never during render.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: Name the legitimate reasons to reach for a DOM ref.
cards.a: Focus management, scrolling, measurement (getBoundingClientRect), media control (play/pause), text selection, and handing a node to a third-party library.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: What must you never do with a DOM node React owns?
cards.a: Add or remove its children yourself. React's picture of the tree becomes wrong and it will eventually clobber you or crash. If you need to hand a subtree to a library, give it a node React renders empty and never touches.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: Why was forwardRef needed, and what changed in React 19?
cards.a: ref was consumed by React rather than passed as a prop, so a ref on your component never reached the DOM node inside; forwardRef delivered it as a second argument. In React 19 ref is an ordinary prop you can destructure, and forwardRef is being retired. Both forms are common in real code.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: What is useImperativeHandle for?
cards.a: Exposing a deliberately narrow API to a parent — { focus, scrollToTop } — instead of the raw DOM node, so a component library does not leak its internal structure.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: What is a ref callback, and what did React 19 add to it?
cards.a: Passing a function to ref instead of a ref object; React calls it with the node on attach and null on detach. React 19 lets it return a cleanup function, called on detach instead of the null call.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: How do you store a list of refs for a dynamic list?
cards.a: One ref holding a Map keyed by item id, populated by ref callbacks — not an array indexed by position, which breaks on reorder for the same reasons index keys do.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: Why is 'refs are a hack, avoid them' wrong?
cards.a: They are the intended escape hatch. Focus, scroll, measurement, and imperative library integration have no declarative form; avoiding refs there produces worse code, usually an effect that fights the DOM.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: What is the gap Node 9 leaves?
cards.a: You now have several hooks that all break if placed inside an if, with no explanation why, and you are copy-pasting the same hook combinations between components with no way to extract them.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: When is ref.current guaranteed to be set?
cards.a: After commit — so in effects and in event handlers. During render it may be null or stale, which is why reading it there is unsafe.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: How do you get the previous value of a prop?
cards.a: Store it in a ref and update the ref in an effect after each render. The ref lags by one render by construction, which is exactly what you want.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: Why prefer a ref over state for a timer id?
cards.a: Because the UI does not display it. Putting it in state would cause a re-render for a value nothing renders.

cards.t: Node 9 · Refs and the escape hatch
cards.q: How do you focus an input as soon as a modal opens?
cards.a: A ref on the input plus an effect that calls .focus() when the modal mounts. Use useLayoutEffect only if the focus jump is visible.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: When did hooks ship?
cards.a: React 16.8, on 6 February 2019. They became the default way to write React and made class components legacy without deprecating them.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What problem did hooks actually solve? (Not verbosity.)
cards.a: Class components could not extract and reuse stateful logic. Lifecycle methods split one concern across three places and mixed three concerns into one method.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What were the pre-hooks reuse patterns and what was wrong with them?
cards.a: Higher-order components and render props. They worked, but each layer added a component to the tree, producing deeply nested 'wrapper hell' that was miserable to read in DevTools.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Explain the mechanism behind hooks.
cards.a: React keeps, per component instance, an ordered list of hook records. When your function runs, React points at that component and at position 0; each hook call reads the record at the current position and advances the pointer. Records are created on the first render and read back in the same order after.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Hooks are matched by what?
cards.a: Call order, not by name. useState has no idea the variable is called count.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Derive the rules of hooks from the mechanism.
cards.a: Only call hooks at the top level, because a hook inside an if, loop, or after an early return changes the call order, so position 2 now holds a different hook's record. And only call them from components or other hooks, because outside a render there is no component whose list to point at.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What error does React throw when hook order changes, and what is the real failure?
cards.a: "Rendered fewer hooks than expected." React detects the count mismatch, but the underlying failure is silent misalignment — one hook reading another's stored value.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What enforces the hook rules in practice?
cards.a: eslint-plugin-react-hooks, which checks the rules of hooks plus exhaustive dependencies. Not optional tooling in a real codebase.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What is a custom hook?
cards.a: Just a function whose name starts with use that calls other hooks. No API, no registration — the prefix exists so the linter applies the rules.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What do custom hooks share, and what do they not share?
cards.a: They share logic, never state. Two components calling useCounter() get two independent counters, because each call site gets its own hook records.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: How do you actually share state between components?
cards.a: Lift it to a common ancestor, put it in context, or put it in a store outside React. A custom hook cannot do it by itself.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Why are custom hooks better than HOCs for reuse?
cards.a: They reuse logic without adding a single level to the component tree — exactly the thing HOCs and render props could not avoid.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Are class components deprecated?
cards.a: No. They still work and appear in every codebase older than 2019. You should be able to read this.state, this.setState, render(), and the main lifecycle methods, and map them onto hooks — but write new code with hooks.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What is the one thing classes can still do that hooks cannot?
cards.a: Be an error boundary, via static getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch. There is no hook equivalent, which is why react-error-boundary exists.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Map the three main class lifecycle methods onto hooks.
cards.a: componentDidMount and componentDidUpdate both map onto useEffect with the right dependencies; componentWillUnmount maps onto the effect's cleanup return. The mapping is imperfect on purpose — the framings differ.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What does useId do and why does it exist?
cards.a: Generates a stable unique id string for accessibility attributes that is consistent between server and client rendering — hand-rolled counters or random ids cause hydration mismatches.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What is useDebugValue?
cards.a: A hook that labels a custom hook's value in React DevTools. Useful in shared libraries, rarely in app code.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Why is the use naming convention load-bearing?
cards.a: It is how the linter knows to enforce the rules of hooks on a function. Naming a hook without the prefix means the rules go unchecked; prefixing a non-hook makes the linter complain incorrectly.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Can a custom hook call another custom hook?
cards.a: Yes, arbitrarily deep. Each one contributes its hook records to the calling component's single ordered list, which is why order still matters across the whole chain.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: What is the smallest useful custom hook and why extract it?
cards.a: Something like useToggle or useLocalStorage — extracted not for line count but because the logic has a name, so call sites become readable and the logic becomes testable on its own.

cards.t: Node 10 · Hooks mechanism and custom hooks
cards.q: Why can use() be called conditionally when hooks cannot?
cards.a: Because it is not implemented as a positional hook record — it is a first-class React API integrated with Suspense. It is deliberately exempt from the rules of hooks.

cards.q: What are the three parts of using context?
cards.a: createContext(default) creates the channel; a provider makes a value available to its subtree; useContext(TheContext) reads the nearest provided value above the reader.

cards.q: What changed about providers in React 19?
cards.a: You can render the context itself: <ThemeContext value={t}> instead of <ThemeContext.Provider value={t}>. Both forms are in the wild.

cards.q: What does the createContext default value do?
cards.a: It is used when a consumer has no matching provider above it. Usually set to something that makes a missing provider loud — or the context is wrapped in a custom hook that throws.

cards.q: Does context let data flow upward or sideways?
cards.a: No. It is still strictly one-way flow — it just skips the intermediate components. A component can only read what an ancestor provided.

cards.q: When does a context consumer re-render?
cards.a: Whenever the provided value changes by Object.is — regardless of which part of the value the consumer actually uses.

cards.q: Why does <AuthContext value={{ user, login, logout }}> destroy performance?
cards.a: The object literal is new on every render of the provider, so every consumer in the app re-renders on every parent render even when nothing meaningful changed.

cards.q: Name two fixes for context over-rendering.
cards.a: useMemo the provided value so its identity is stable; or split one context into two — a rarely-changing one for dispatch functions and a frequently-changing one for data — so action-only consumers don't re-render.

cards.q: Why is context not a state manager?
cards.a: It solves transport only. It has no update model, no batching, and no way for a consumer to subscribe to one field. That gap is what Zustand, Redux Toolkit, and Jotai fill.

cards.q: Answer 'why use Redux instead of context?' properly.
cards.a: Selective subscription (components re-render only for the slice they read), a predictable single update model, devtools with time-travel, and middleware. Not because 'context is slow' — that is usually an unstable provider value.

cards.q: What is context genuinely good for?
cards.a: Values that are global and change rarely: theme, current user, locale, feature flags, router state — and well-scoped shared state for one subtree.

cards.q: What is the common wrapper pattern for a context?
cards.a: Export a provider component plus a useAuth() hook that calls useContext and throws if the value is missing, so misuse fails loudly instead of returning the default.

cards.q: What is the gap Node 11 leaves?
cards.a: Everything so far is about where state lives, never how it changes. Eight setters scattered across a dozen handlers means there is no single place to read the rules, and invalid combinations creep back in.

cards.q: What does React do if there is no provider above a consumer?
cards.a: It uses the default value passed to createContext. If that default is null, downstream code usually crashes further away from the real cause — which is why a throwing custom hook is the standard guard.

cards.q: Does a context provider re-render its children when the value changes?
cards.a: It re-renders consumers. Children that don't call useContext re-render only for the usual reason — their parent rendered. Passing subtrees as children keeps them out of it.

cards.q: Can you have two providers for the same context in one tree?
cards.a: Yes, and nesting is a feature: the nearest provider above the consumer wins, which is how per-subtree overrides (a dark section inside a light page) work.

cards.q: What is a reducer, precisely?
cards.a: A pure function (state, action) => newState. Given the same state and action it always returns the same next state and touches nothing else.

cards.q: What are the pieces of useReducer?
cards.a: const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState). An action is a plain object describing what happened, conventionally { type: 'added', payload }. dispatch(action) hands it to React, which calls your reducer and re-renders.

cards.q: What is the framing shift from setters to a reducer?
cards.a: Components stop setting values and start reporting events. One function decides what each event means.

cards.q: Name four concrete benefits of a reducer over scattered setters.
cards.a: All transition logic in one readable place; it's a pure function so it is testable with no rendering; impossible states become unrepresentable since the reducer is the only writer; and the action list reads as a log of everything the feature can do.

cards.q: What is guaranteed about dispatch's identity?
cards.a: It is stable across renders. So passing it through props or context never causes identity-based re-render problems, and it can be safely omitted from dependency arrays.

cards.q: When do you move from useState to useReducer?
cards.a: When several state values change together, when the next state depends non-trivially on the previous, when the same update logic is triggered from many places, or when you keep writing the same three setters in a row. The signal is the number of related transitions, not the number of variables.

cards.q: What is the useReducer + context pattern?
cards.a: Hold the state at the top with a reducer, put state in one context and dispatch in another, and any depth of component can read or dispatch without prop drilling and without a library. It covers a large share of what people install Redux for.

cards.q: How does Redux relate to useReducer?
cards.a: Same shape, made global: one store for the app, plus middleware and devtools. Modern Redux means Redux Toolkit, which uses immer so reducers look mutating while producing new state.

cards.q: Can a reducer perform a side effect?
cards.a: No — it must stay pure. Fetching, logging, and timers belong in handlers, effects, or middleware. An impure reducer breaks under StrictMode double-invocation and under concurrent rendering.

cards.q: What is the third argument of useReducer for?
cards.a: A lazy init function: useReducer(reducer, initialArg, init) calls init(initialArg) once to build initial state, which keeps expensive setup out of every render and gives you a reusable 'reset' function.

cards.q: How does a reducer close Node 6's contradictory-state hole?
cards.a: By making the transitions explicit: there is no action that produces loading && error, because each action returns one complete, valid next state rather than mutating one flag at a time.

cards.q: What is the gap Node 12 leaves?
cards.a: Correctness is handled; cost is not. Every state change re-renders a subtree, controlled inputs render per keystroke, context re-renders every consumer — and you have no framework for reasoning about why the app feels slow.

cards.q: Where should the reducer function live?
cards.a: Outside the component, at module scope. It has no dependency on props or state, so defining it inside means recreating it on every render for no reason and inviting accidental closure over stale values.

cards.q: How do you test a reducer?
cards.a: Call it directly with a state and an action and assert on the returned state. No rendering, no DOM, no React — which is a large part of the point.

cards.q: What does an action's type field buy you over calling a method?
cards.a: A serialisable record of what happened, which is what makes logging, devtools, time-travel, and replay possible.

cards.q: State the default re-render rule exactly.
cards.a: When a component re-renders, all of its descendants re-render — not because their props changed, but because their parent rendered. React does not check props unless you asked it to.

cards.q: Why is that usually fine?
cards.a: Running a function that returns objects is cheap, and React only touches the DOM where the description actually differs. Rendering is not painting.

cards.q: When does the default rule stop being fine?
cards.a: When a component does real work per render (large lists, heavy formatting, charts), when the subtree is very large, or when the state changes very often — a keystroke, scroll, drag, or mousemove.

cards.q: What does React.memo do?
cards.a: Wraps a component so React skips re-rendering it when its props are shallowly equal to last time — each prop compared with Object.is, one level deep.

cards.q: What does useMemo do?
cards.a: Caches the result of a computation between renders, recomputing only when a dependency changes. Used for genuinely expensive computation and for keeping an object or array's identity stable.

cards.q: What does useCallback do, and what is it equivalent to?
cards.a: Caches a function so the same identity is handed down across renders. It is exactly useMemo(() => fn, deps) with nicer syntax.

cards.q: What is referential identity and why does it govern all three tools?
cards.a: Every object literal, array literal, and arrow function inside a component is created anew on each render, and {a:1} === {a:1} is false. So memoisation only works if the values being compared keep the same identity.

cards.q: Why does <MemoList items={tasks.filter(f)} onSelect={() => ...} /> gain nothing from memo?
cards.a: Both props are new values every render, so the shallow comparison always fails. You added comparison cost for zero benefit — one of the most common wasted optimisations in real code.

cards.q: Which three separate symptoms all trace back to referential identity?
cards.a: React.memo never bailing out; an effect re-running every render; and a context provider re-rendering all consumers. Same mechanism, three faces.

cards.q: Why should you not memoise by default?
cards.a: useMemo and useCallback allocate, store, and compare dependencies, and they make code harder to read. Optimising a component that takes 0.2 ms is worse than doing nothing.

cards.q: What tool tells you what to optimise?
cards.a: The React DevTools Profiler, which shows which components rendered, why they rendered, and how long each took. Measure before memoising.

cards.q: What is the React Compiler and what does it change?
cards.a: A build-time compiler (announced 2024, 1.0 in late 2025) that analyses components and inserts memoisation automatically wherever it is safe, provided your code follows the Rules of React. Where adopted, most hand-written useMemo/useCallback becomes unnecessary.

cards.q: Why do you still need to understand manual memoisation?
cards.a: Because most existing codebases have not adopted the compiler, and because reading and reviewing them requires knowing when a memo is load-bearing and when it is noise.

cards.q: Name three structural optimisations that beat memoisation.
cards.a: Move state down into the smallest component that needs it; pass expensive subtrees as children so they are created by a parent that isn't re-rendering; and virtualise long lists so only visible rows exist in the DOM.

cards.q: What is list virtualisation and when do you need it?
cards.a: Rendering only the rows currently in the viewport (plus a small overscan), via react-window or TanStack Virtual. Needed once a list is long enough that the DOM node count itself is the cost — typically hundreds to thousands of rows.

cards.q: Does React.memo do a deep comparison?
cards.a: No — shallow, one level, with Object.is per prop. You can pass a custom comparison function as the second argument, but a deep compare is usually more expensive than the render you're avoiding.

cards.q: Why does passing children as a prop avoid re-renders?
cards.a: The children elements were created by the parent, so if the parent doesn't re-render, those element objects keep their identity and React can skip that subtree even though the intermediate component re-rendered.

cards.q: What is the gap Node 13 leaves?
cards.a: Memoisation cannot help when the work genuinely must happen — filtering fifty thousand rows. Once React starts rendering it will not stop, so the keystroke that triggered it cannot be shown until it finishes, and the input freezes.

cards.q: Predict: you wrap a child in memo and pass it onClick={handleClick} where handleClick is declared in the parent body. Does memo work?
cards.a: No. The function is recreated every render, so the shallow prop comparison fails. Wrap it in useCallback — or adopt the React Compiler and stop hand-writing this.

cards.q: Why does useMemo not guarantee the value is cached?
cards.a: React reserves the right to discard memoised values — for example under memory pressure or in future features. It is a performance hint, not a semantic guarantee, so never rely on it for correctness.

cards.q: What is the difference between a component re-rendering and the DOM updating?
cards.a: Re-rendering runs your function and produces new element objects. The DOM only changes where the new description differs from the old. Most re-renders produce zero DOM operations.

cards.q: How do you read 'why did this render' in the Profiler?
cards.a: Enable 'Record why each component rendered' in DevTools settings; the profiler then labels each render with the cause — props changed (and which), state changed, context changed, or parent rendered.

cards.q: What is concurrent rendering, in one sentence?
cards.a: React's ability to begin rendering, pause partway, handle something more urgent, and then resume or discard the partial work — made possible by fiber and exposed in React 18.

cards.q: Why can partial rendering work be discarded safely?
cards.a: Because React renders into an in-progress tree and only commits when a render completes. Nothing half-updated ever reaches the screen.

cards.q: What is the actual point of concurrency? (Not 'speed'.)
cards.a: Not all updates are equally urgent. A keystroke must appear immediately; a filtered list of fifty thousand results can lag. Before React 18 there was no way to express that difference, so the cheap update queued behind the expensive one.

cards.q: What does useTransition give you?
cards.a: const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(). Updates inside startTransition are marked non-urgent; React renders urgent updates first and does transition work in interruptible chunks, abandoning it if a newer update arrives. isPending lets you dim stale results.

cards.q: How does React keep the browser responsive during a transition?
cards.a: It yields control back to the browser between chunks — roughly every 5 milliseconds — so input and painting can happen inside the ~16.7 ms frame budget.

cards.q: What is useDeferredValue and when do you use it instead of useTransition?
cards.a: const deferred = useDeferredValue(value) gives a copy that lags behind during heavy work. Use it when you do not control the state update — for example the value arrives as a prop. Render the input from the live value and the expensive list from the deferred one.

cards.q: What is required for concurrent features to work at all?
cards.a: The React 18 createRoot entry point. An app still on legacy ReactDOM.render runs in a compatibility mode with concurrency disabled.

cards.q: What is the lane model?
cards.a: React's internal priority system: updates are tagged with a lane, lanes are processed in priority order, with starvation protection so a low-priority update cannot be postponed forever. You never touch it directly.

cards.q: Name the honest limits of concurrent rendering.
cards.a: It only helps when the bottleneck is rendering. It does nothing for a slow network request or a slow API, and it does not make any single render faster.

cards.q: Why did purity become non-negotiable with concurrency?
cards.a: Because a render may now run twice, be interrupted, or be thrown away entirely. An impure component that got away with it under React 17's uninterrupted rendering can genuinely break under React 18.

cards.q: What does StrictMode's double-render in development detect?
cards.a: Impure render functions — mutating props or state, writing to outer variables, or producing different output from the same inputs. It surfaces exactly the class of bug concurrency would otherwise expose in production.

cards.q: Is a transition the same as a debounce?
cards.a: No. A debounce delays starting the work by a fixed time. A transition starts immediately at low priority and is interrupted by newer urgent work, so it is both faster in the quiet case and responsive in the busy case.

cards.q: Which state updates are urgent by default?
cards.a: All of them. Everything is urgent unless you explicitly mark it with startTransition or consume it through useDeferredValue.

cards.q: Can you mark a controlled input's own state update as a transition?
cards.a: No — that is the one thing you must keep urgent, or typing lags. Keep the input's state urgent and defer only the expensive downstream work.

cards.q: What is tearing and which hook exists to prevent it?
cards.a: Two parts of one screen rendering different versions of the same external store, possible because a render can be interrupted while the store changes underneath. useSyncExternalStore exists to prevent it.

cards.q: What does React.lazy(() => import('./Chart')) do?
cards.a: Produces a component whose code is only downloaded the first time it renders. The dynamic import() is a signal the bundler recognises: it splits that module and its imports into a separate file.

cards.q: What is code splitting and where do you split first?
cards.a: Breaking the bundle into chunks fetched on demand. Split by route first — a user on the login page does not need the admin dashboard's charting library.

cards.q: What does <Suspense fallback={...}> do?
cards.a: Declares a boundary. If anything inside it suspends — waiting for code or data — React shows the fallback for that region only, leaving the rest of the page alone, and swaps in real content when ready.

cards.q: What is the conceptual shift Suspense introduces?
cards.a: The parent declares the loading UI for a region, instead of every leaf managing its own spinner. That makes coordinated loading states possible — one fallback for a group arriving together, rather than six spinners popping in at different moments.

cards.q: How has Suspense's scope grown?
cards.a: It started as code-splitting only, gained server-side data support in React 18, and with React 19's use() API works with promises on the client — which is why data libraries increasingly express loading through Suspense rather than booleans.

cards.q: What does React do with an uncaught render error, and why?
cards.a: It unmounts the whole tree, producing a blank page. The deliberate reasoning since React 16 is that a visibly broken app is safer than a silently corrupted one.

cards.q: What is an error boundary and how is it implemented?
cards.a: A component that catches errors from its subtree and renders a fallback, containing damage to one region. Implemented with the class methods static getDerivedStateFromError (render the fallback) and componentDidCatch (log it).

cards.q: Why does almost nobody write an error boundary class by hand?
cards.a: Because it is the one thing hooks cannot do, so the ecosystem standardised on react-error-boundary, which wraps it with a hook-friendly API and a reset mechanism.

cards.q: What do error boundaries not catch?
cards.a: Errors inside event handlers (not during render — use try/catch), errors in async code, errors thrown by the boundary itself, and errors during server rendering.

cards.q: What did React 19 add around error handling?
cards.a: Root options onCaughtError and onUncaughtError, and much better hydration mismatch messages that show an actual diff instead of a generic warning.

cards.q: What is <Activity>?
cards.a: Added in React 19.2 (October 2025). It keeps part of the tree mounted but hidden, preserving its state while deprioritising its rendering — the long-requested 'keep the previous tab alive' capability.

cards.q: Where should Suspense and error boundaries sit in a tree?
cards.a: Around meaningful regions, usually one layer above the thing that can fail or wait — per route, per panel, per widget — so one failure or delay degrades a section rather than the page.

cards.q: What is the gap Node 15 leaves?
cards.a: The shape is still an empty HTML file plus a large JavaScript bundle. The user sees nothing until it downloads and runs, crawlers and link previews see nothing, and every byte of data still needs a round trip after the app has loaded.

cards.q: What happens if a component suspends with no Suspense boundary above it?
cards.a: React walks up looking for one; with none, it errors. In practice every framework provides a root boundary, but an unwrapped lazy component in a plain app throws.

cards.q: Why does a Suspense fallback sometimes flash for a few milliseconds?
cards.a: The content resolved almost immediately but the boundary still switched to the fallback. Transitions avoid this: an update inside startTransition keeps showing the old UI instead of falling back.

cards.q: How do error boundaries and Suspense boundaries compose?
cards.a: An error boundary wrapping a Suspense boundary handles both waiting and failing for the same region — the standard pairing in route-level layouts.

cards.q: What is server-side rendering?
cards.a: Running your components on the server to produce an HTML string that is sent in the first response, so the user sees real content before any JavaScript has run.

cards.q: What is hydration?
cards.a: The browser loads the same JavaScript, React renders the tree, and instead of creating DOM nodes it walks the existing server HTML and attaches event handlers and state to the nodes already there. Entry point: hydrateRoot, not createRoot.

cards.q: What does SSR actually buy you?
cards.a: Faster first paint and content that crawlers and link previews can read. It does not make the app faster overall.

cards.q: What is a hydration mismatch and what causes it?
cards.a: The server HTML and the client's first render disagree. Caused by new Date(), Math.random(), window.innerWidth, locale-dependent formatting, and anything read from localStorage.

cards.q: How do you fix a hydration mismatch?
cards.a: Render the varying part only after mount (state flipped in an effect), or use suppressHydrationWarning for a genuinely unavoidable case like a rendered timestamp.

cards.q: Why does module-level window access crash SSR?
cards.a: There is no window or document on the server. Access must be inside effects or guarded, since effects never run during server rendering.

cards.q: Why can SSR feel worse than client rendering to a user?
cards.a: Time-to-interactive lags first paint: the page looks ready and does not respond until hydration finishes, so the user clicks and nothing happens.

cards.q: What does SSR not fix?
cards.a: Bundle size. You still ship every component's JavaScript to the client, including purely static ones. That is the gap server components close.

cards.q: What is a React Server Component?
cards.a: A component that runs only on the server, once, and never ships its JavaScript to the browser. It can await directly in the body — query a database, read a file, use secrets — and what reaches the client is a serialised description of its output, not HTML and not a bundle.

cards.q: Name three consequences of RSC.
cards.a: No client JavaScript for static parts; no API layer needed for a component's own data, which kills a large class of waterfalls; and a genuinely smaller bundle.

cards.q: What can a server component not do?
cards.a: Use state, effects, refs, context, or event handlers — none of which mean anything without a browser.

cards.q: What does 'use client' do?
cards.a: Marks the boundary where server rendering stops and client code begins. That file and everything it imports ship to the browser.

cards.q: What does 'use server' do, and why is it confused with 'use client'?
cards.a: It marks a server function (previously 'server action') — code that runs on the server but is callable from client code, with React wiring up the request. It is not the opposite of 'use client'; they describe different things.

cards.q: Can you adopt RSC by installing React?
cards.a: No. It became stable in React 19 but needs a framework with bundler integration — in practice Next.js App Router or React Router v7 / Remix. That is the honest reason 'learn React, then Next.js' is the standard path.

cards.q: Name the rendering strategies on the spectrum.
cards.a: Client-side rendering; server-side rendering per request; static generation at build time; incremental/on-demand regeneration; streaming SSR; and server components. Being able to say what each costs and buys is high-value in an interview.

cards.q: What is streaming SSR?
cards.a: The server sends HTML in chunks as it becomes ready rather than waiting for the whole page, using Suspense boundaries as the flush points — so slow data does not hold up the fast parts of the page.

cards.q: What is the difference between SSR and static generation?
cards.a: SSR renders per request, so it can use request-specific data and is always fresh. Static generation renders once at build time and serves a file, which is fastest and cheapest but stale until rebuilt.

cards.q: Why do server components reduce waterfalls?
cards.a: Because a server component fetches its own data on the server, close to the database, and nested components' fetches happen in the same render pass on the same machine rather than as sequential browser round trips.

cards.q: Can a server component render a client component and vice versa?
cards.a: A server component can render client components. A client component cannot import a server component, but it can render one passed to it as children or a prop — which is the standard way to keep server content inside a client shell.

cards.q: What actually crosses the network from a server component to the client?
cards.a: A serialised stream describing the rendered output and the client component references and props. Props must therefore be serialisable — you cannot pass a function or a class instance across that boundary.

cards.q: What is React's actual scope?
cards.a: A library for building user interfaces out of components. It renders a tree. Routing, data, forms, styling, and testing are deliberately not included.

cards.q: What are the routing options and what is the underlying mechanism?
cards.a: React Router (the default; from v7 it absorbed Remix and can be a full framework), TanStack Router (type-safe), or a framework's own router. Mechanically: intercept navigation, update the URL with the History API without a page load, render a different tree.

cards.q: Why do deep links 404 in a client-routed SPA, and how do you fix it?
cards.a: The browser asks the server for /settings, which has no such file. Configure the server (or host) to serve index.html for every unmatched path so the client router can take over.

cards.q: What is the mature answer to 'which state manager do you use'?
cards.a: Separate server cache from client state. Most apps that reached for Redux only ever needed the former — TanStack Query. For real client state: context plus reducer, Zustand, Redux Toolkit, or an atomic library like Jotai.

cards.q: How do Zustand and Redux Toolkit differ in practice?
cards.a: Zustand is small, hook-based, and needs no provider — you create a store and select from it. Redux Toolkit brings one global store, strong conventions, middleware, and time-travel devtools, which pays off in large teams and large apps.

cards.q: Why is React Hook Form fast?
cards.a: It keeps inputs uncontrolled and subscribes via refs, so typing does not re-render the form — directly attacking the per-keystroke render cost of controlled inputs.

cards.q: What pairs with React Hook Form for validation?
cards.a: Zod schemas via a resolver — the same validation library you can use on the server, so one schema defines the contract on both ends.

cards.q: What is the current styling landscape?
cards.a: Tailwind is the default; CSS Modules and vanilla-extract are solid alternatives; runtime CSS-in-JS is declining specifically because it works badly with server components.

cards.q: What is shadcn/ui and why is it unusual?
cards.a: Not a dependency — a generator that copies accessible Radix-based components into your own repo, so you own and edit the code. It is the current mainstream for building a design system quickly.

cards.q: What replaced Create React App and when?
cards.a: Vite. CRA was formally deprecated in February 2025. Scaffolding a React app in 2026 means Vite or a framework; knowing CRA is dead is a currency signal.

cards.q: State React Testing Library's philosophy.
cards.a: Test what the user experiences. Query by accessible role and visible text, never by class name or component internals, so a refactor that changes structure but not behaviour does not break the suite.

cards.q: What is the standard React testing stack?
cards.a: React Testing Library with Vitest (or Jest) for component tests, user-event for realistic interaction, MSW for mocking network at the request level, and Playwright for end-to-end.

cards.q: Why is TypeScript effectively mandatory for React in 2026?
cards.a: Typed props are the single largest quality win available to a React codebase — they make component contracts explicit and catch the entire class of 'wrong prop shape' bugs that props' dynamism otherwise allows.

cards.q: How do you answer 'how would you structure a React app'?
cards.a: Name the choices and defend each: build tool, router, server-state library, client-state approach, form library, styling, component layer, testing. The answer is the reasoning, not the list.

cards.q: What does 'React is a library, not a framework' mean for an interview answer?
cards.a: That every architectural decision — routing, data, state, forms, styling, testing — is yours to make and defend. Frameworks like Next.js exist precisely to make those choices for you.

cards.q: How do you decide between a framework (Next.js) and Vite plus libraries?
cards.a: Framework if you want SSR/RSC, file-based routing, and deployment conventions handed to you. Vite plus libraries if the app is a client-side dashboard behind a login, where SEO and first-paint are irrelevant and you want fewer constraints.

cards.q: What is the minimum accessible-React knowledge worth having?
cards.a: Use semantic elements so roles come for free, label every input, keep focus managed in modals and after navigation, and never remove focus outlines without a replacement. Testing Library's role-based queries push you toward this by default.
